papers.title_in_file: Loss Behavior in Supervised Learning with Entangled States
papers.what_it_is: A theory-plus-simulation paper showing that, when learning a unitary with a maximally entangled training sample, the distance to a global minimum is larger and the loss improvement in a bounded neighborhood is exponentially smaller than with a separable sample, with simulated PQC experiments and a study of non-maximally entangled samples.

existing.value: The authors state that, in their simplified setting (optimization over all unitaries with the phase-corrected Frobenius-norm metric), the possible improvement of the loss in a constrained neighborhood scales inversely with the dimension of the state space. papers.what_it_is: A proposed quantum algorithm that maps graph nodes to qubits and edges to non-unitary two-qubit ZX-calculus Z spiders, so each connected component becomes a GHZ state that two measurements can test, with depth bounds, a state-decay analysis and a Julia/Yao simulation.

existing.note: The constant-measurement claim holds only when the state decay caused by the non-unitary spiders is removed with ancilla qubits (up to one per edge) or ignored; without ancillas the paper states exponentially many measurements are needed (Table II gives order two to the n). The three-quarters figure is the worst case of two fragments with two measurements.
existing.value: The authors introduce a quantum algorithm for determining graph connectedness using a constant number of measurements, and state that it needs only two measurements to compute the result with a certainty of p = 3/4 (the worst case of two graph fragments). They also state that the non-unitary operations cause a state decay that either requires an exponential number of measurements as the number of qubits grows or needs ancilla qubits.

papers.what_it_is: A perspective paper that classifies parametrized quantum circuits by whether their output function families are classically evaluatable (Property 1) and identifiable from parameters (Property 2), maps shallow, low-doping, free-fermionic and flipped architectures onto three nested classes, and proves that ERM over the relaxed Class 2 family is classically easy while ERM over the quantum-parametrized family is QCMA-complete in the worst case.
